chapter: Return to New York, addiction, health and the NBC job
title: Clarifying the Feather fight: the record ban and the song 'When the Sun Comes Out'
summary: The altercation fell in the 1942-44 recording ban, when the black-market date left him unable to testify.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: I think there was something else you wanted to add to the story --

Yes, to try to clarify the story with Leonard Feather and our altercation. This took place during the record ban, which was between '42 and '44, as you say. And it was either late '43 or early '44 that it happened. Because I had came to California in the Spring of '44 with Big Sid Catlett's group. You know, when this had happened, or shortly before.
And so what you were saying, the reason you couldn't testify in Court --

Oh, the reasons I couldn't testify in Court was because this was a black market record date, you know. We wasn't supposed to be recording. And Big-Ben asked for his price and it was confirmed. Sid asked for his price, it was confirmed. I asked for my price and it was confirmed. So when he filed charges on me, and I had to go to court, I couldn't tell the story. I was handcuffed, because if I had told that I had recorded with Big Sid and Ben on the record date, they would have been thrown out of the union as well as myself.
Did Parrish get paid, do you know?
I doubt it. I doubt it.
You said that you also remembered the name of the number that Big Sid used to --
Oh, yeah. (Singing), 'When the sun comes out,' but they built up this big introduction, you know, and they'd leave a space open and he'd say, 'Quit your squawking,
The name of that number was "When the Sun Comes Out"?
Yeah. And then when we got to the exhibition grounds in Toronto, he said, "TWA, take it away."
